messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 79
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
- Pcl5: 42

# Vignette: Samuel

Samuel is a 79-year-old man of African descent who has spent the better part of six decades moving boxes, stacking pallets, and keeping inventory at a regional warehouse on the outskirts of the city. He has worked there longer than most of his current colleagues have been alive, and he takes a quiet pride in that. He comes in early, keeps to himself, and does what needs to be done. His supervisors describe him as dependable. Samuel would say the same of himself. Dependability, he believes, is what separates a man from what he grew up around.

What he grew up around was his father's fists.

From the time Samuel was roughly five until he was fourteen, he watched his father beat his mother with a regularity that felt, in the way that terrible things can feel to a child, almost ordinary. The sounds are what stayed with him — the particular crack of a hand against a face, his mother's muffled crying through a wall she pressed herself against, the strange silence afterward that was somehow worse than the noise. He remembers standing in the doorway of the kitchen one evening, perhaps eight years old, watching his father drag his mother across the linoleum floor by her wrist, and feeling his own body go completely still. He did not run. He did not speak. He stood there until it was over, and then he went to bed. He has never fully forgiven himself for that stillness.

His mother died when Samuel was in his late twenties — causes unrelated to the violence, though he has never been entirely convinced of that. His father outlived her by fifteen years. Samuel did not attend the funeral.

He married in his thirties and divorced in his fifties. His ex-wife, a woman he describes with genuine warmth and evident regret, told him near the end that he was never really present. That he would disappear inside himself without warning, sometimes mid-conversation, and come back somewhere else entirely. He knew she was right. He just did not know what to do about it.

Now, at 79, the disappearing happens more frequently. He will be loading a shipment and hear a younger colleague raise his voice across the warehouse floor — not even in anger, just in the ordinary loud way young men speak — and something in Samuel's chest seizes. His hands go cold. He sets down whatever he is carrying and finds a reason to step outside. He stands in the loading dock and breathes until the feeling passes, which sometimes takes a long time.

He sleeps poorly. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning with a heaviness in his chest that he cannot name precisely but recognizes as old. On the worst nights there are dreams — not always of his father directly, but of dark rooms, of being unable to move, of sounds he cannot locate. He lies awake afterward and listens to the silence of his apartment and tells himself it was a long time ago. This helps only a little.

He has begun avoiding the television in the evenings. Too many programs show men and women arguing, and even the suggestion of escalating conflict — a raised voice, a slammed door — sends something cold through him that takes hours to settle. He eats dinner early and goes to bed with the radio on low, tuned to a station that plays older music. This is the closest thing to comfort he has found.

What troubles Samuel most, sitting across from the therapist in a chair he chose specifically because it faces the door, is not the dreams or the sleeplessness or the way loud voices still reach inside him after all these years. What troubles him is the suspicion, quiet but persistent, that the small, still boy in the kitchen doorway never really left. That he has been carrying that child through every warehouse, every marriage, every silent decade — and that the child is still waiting, in some room Samuel cannot quite reach, for something to finally be different.
